findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. The spouse is a partner (or a sole proprietor) whose partnership or business runs a dependent care assistance program that paid for their child's 2025 daycare. The spouse's Schedule K-1 shows box 13 code O. The filer has W-2 wages with an empty box 10.
findings.why_no: The gate extends to the spouse only for the employer: 'your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) employer, or your own business or partnership'. The parenthetical does not reach 'your own business or partnership', so the filer truthfully answers no, because the business or partnership is the spouse's, not theirs.
findings.line: scope.care_benefits_other_if_benefits (forced false, so the refusal for non-box-10 benefits never happens and Part III line 12/22/24 amounts are silently dropped)
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: 'if you (or your spouse if filing jointly) received any dependent care benefits for 2025, you must use Form 2441'; i2441 p. 5, Line 12: 'If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did an employer, business or partnership of yours (or, on a joint return, of your spouse) pay for or provide care for a child, dependent or disabled spouse, including through a dependent care account (FSA) or money left in a 2024 account?' Also say in the help that a K-1 code O or W-2 box 10 issued to either spouse counts.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) who left an employer in late 2024 and had no 2025 election, or works for a different employer in 2025. In January to March 2025 they used the leftover 2024 dependent care FSA balance under the old plan's grace period.
findings.why_no: 'In 2025, did your ... employer ... help pay' reads as the current or 2025 employer, and the money was set aside in 2024. The help mentions 'money left in a 2024 dependent care account', but a filer with no 2025 employer, or a new employer that offered nothing, reads 'your employer' as not including the former one.
findings.line: scope.care_benefits_other_if_benefits (grace-period amount belongs on Form 2441 line 13, which should trigger the refusal)
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 13: 'your employer may have permitted you to carry forward any unused amount from 2024 to use during a grace period in 2025 ... Enter on line 13 the amount you carried forward and used in 2025 during the grace period.'
findings.fix: Add to the question: 'including any employer, current or former, or money from a 2024 dependent care account (yours or your spouse's) used in 2025 under a grace period.'

findings.who: A limited partner or small-percentage LLC member in a partnership that offers a dependent care assistance program to its partners. The partnership reimbursed their 2025 child care, and the K-1 shows box 13 code O.
findings.why_no: 'your own business or partnership' reads as a partnership the filer owns or runs. A passive or minority partner does not think of the firm as 'my own partnership'. They also may not see 'help pay' in a reimbursement they think of as a partnership perk or draw.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Definitions: 'Benefits you received as a partner should be shown in box 13 of your Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) with code O.'
findings.fix: Replace 'your own business or partnership' with 'a business you own, or any partnership or LLC you are a partner or member in'. State in the question text, not only in the help, that a K-1 with box 13 code O for either spouse means Yes.

findings.who: A sole proprietor who set up a dependent care assistance program in their own business and had the business pay their child's 2025 care. No W-2 or K-1 shows it.
findings.why_no: 'help pay' suggests someone else contributing, but the money is the filer's own. The help names only W-2 box 10 and K-1 code O as places that 'show it', so a filer with no form may conclude there is nothing to report.
findings.irs_text: f2441 p. 2, line 22: 'Is any amount on line 12 or 13 from your sole proprietorship or partnership?'; i2441 p. 5, Line 12: 'include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship'
findings.fix: Use 'pay for or provide' instead of 'help pay for'. Add to the help: 'If your own business paid for this care under a dependent care plan, answer Yes even though no form reports it.'

findings.who: A sole proprietor or partner whose program paid for day care of a disabled parent who lived with them. The parent had $5,200 or more of gross income, so the filer cannot claim them as a dependent.
findings.why_no: The gate lists 'a child, a dependent or a disabled spouse'. The parent is not the filer's dependent and not a spouse, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Qualifying Person(s): 'Any disabled person who wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves who lived with you for more than half the year and whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except: a. The disabled person had gross income of $5,200 or more'
findings.fix: Say 'care of a child, a dependent, or any other person (including a spouse or parent) who couldn't care for themselves'.

locators: Form 2441 (2025), Part I, "Did you receive dependent care benefits? No. Complete only Part II below. Yes. Complete Part III on page 2 next."; , Purpose of Form

p. 24, Line 1e, "Dependent care benefits should be shown in box 10 of your Form(s) W-2"; , Line 12, "include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership"; , Line 13, "Enter on line 13 the amount you carried forward and used in 2025 during the grace period"

findings.who: A divorced custodial parent paid daycare for her 8-year-old, who lived with her for most of 2025. She signed Form 8332, so the other parent claims the child and the child is not listed as a dependent on her return.
findings.why_no: She reads "a person other than your child under 13" as the whole test. The care was for her own child under 13, so she answers no. She may also take "listed as a dependent" to cover the other parent's return, where the child is listed.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if: ... You were the child's custodial parent."
findings.fix: Ask about the dependent list first: "Was any of the care for someone who is NOT listed as a dependent on this return, including your own child whom the other parent claims?" Make it a separate question from the age test.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly paid care for the wife's 10-year-old from a prior marriage. The child lives with them, but the child's other parent claims the child under a release, so the child is not listed on the joint return.
findings.why_no: "Your child" reads as the child of the person answering. The husband answers as the first filer and thinks of the child as his stepchild or as his spouse's child. Or the couple treats the child as "our child under 13" and answers no without checking whether the child is listed.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if ... You were the child's custodial parent."
findings.fix: Say "your or your spouse's child" and ask directly: "not listed as a dependent on this return".

findings.who: A custodial parent paid care for a child who cannot care for themselves. The child turned 13 in March 2025, and the other parent claims the child.
findings.why_no: "Under 13" has no date. The child was under 13 for part of 2025, when care began, so the filer answers no. The same thing happens if the child is wrongly still on the tool's dependent list.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "The child was under age 13 or wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves"; p503 p. 3: "You determine a person's qualifying status each day."
findings.fix: Ask whether any care was for someone not listed as a dependent or for anyone after their 13th birthday.

findings.who: A 23-year-old graduate student files her own return. Her parents could claim her but chose not to. She pays care for a disabled adult relative who lives with her.
findings.why_no: "Can someone claim you" reads as "did someone claim you", so she answers no. The other helper usually still catches her, because the relative is not a child under 13 listed as a dependent.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "c. You (or your spouse if filing jointly) could be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2025 tax return."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Answer yes if someone could claim you, even if they chose not to."

locators: p. 1, Qualifying Person(s), "or could claim as a dependent except: a. The disabled person had gross income of $5,200 or more, b. The disabled person filed a joint return, or c. You (or your spouse if filing jointly) could be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2025 tax return"; p. 1, Special rule for children of divorced or separated parents or parents who live apart, "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if"; , Birth or death of otherwise qualifying person, "a person who was born or died in 2025 is treated as having lived with you for more than half of 2025 if your home was the person's home more than half the time they were alive in 2025"

findings.who: A married filer on a separate return who took dependent care benefits through a cafeteria plan. They lived apart from their spouse only from September, or their spouse paid most of the household costs, or the child lived mainly with the spouse. They check line A because they read 'meet the requirements to claim the credit' as items 2 through 5.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from line A. The line A instruction asks whether you 'meet the requirements to claim the credit', and a filer can read that as the general items 2-5 or as 'separated'. They check the box without meeting all three unmarried tests, and the computed gate turns false.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 19: 'Are you considered unmarried under that rule? ... No. Enter your spouse's earned income on line 19'; p. 2: 'You lived apart from your spouse during the last 6 months of 2025. • Your home was the qualifying person's main home for more than half of 2025. • You paid more than half of the cost of keeping up that home'
findings.fix: Do not compute the gate from a bare line A checkbox. Ask the three tests as separate factual questions (lived apart every day July through December 2025; child's main home was yours more than half the year; you paid more than half the home's upkeep), and set line A only when all three are yes.

findings.who: A married filer on a separate return, not considered unmarried, who claims the dependent care exclusion. Their spouse is a deployed service member whose pay is mostly nontaxable combat pay (W-2 box 12 code Q), with little or no box 1 wages.
findings.why_no: The question says 'Count wages and net earnings from self-employment'. The filer counts box 1 wages only and leaves out combat pay, which can be elected into earned income. They enter zero or a small amount, which caps the exclusion wrongly.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 18: 'You can elect to include your nontaxable combat pay in earned income when figuring your exclusion or deduction ... (line 19 for your spouse if filing jointly)'
findings.fix: Ask separately whether the spouse received nontaxable combat pay (W-2 box 12 code Q), and resolve whether the election applies on a separate return. If it is unclear, stop and refuse rather than taking the amount as zero.

findings.who: A married filer on a separate return whose spouse was enrolled full time for one semester (five calendar months), or was disabled for part of the year. The filer reads the help text 'A Yes ends the interview here' and wants to finish the return.
findings.why_no: The help warns that a yes ends the interview, which pushes the filer toward no. A filer who is unsure whether a partial-year disability or one semester 'counts' picks no to continue. The refusal is then missed, and the spouse's earned income is taken without the $250/$500-per-month deemed amount.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 4: 'For each month or part of a month your spouse was a student or was disabled, they are considered to have worked and earned income. Their earned income for each month is considered to be at least $250 ($500 ...)'
findings.fix: Remove 'A Yes ends the interview here' from the help. State the test neutrally: 'Count any month in which your spouse was disabled for any part of the month, or enrolled full time for some part of each of at least 5 months in 2025.'

findings.who: A married filer on a separate return, not considered unmarried, who was a full-time student themselves for five months in 2025. Their spouse was neither a student nor disabled.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks only about 'your husband or wife'. The filer truthfully answers no, but the line 19 instruction points to the deemed-income rules if 'you or your spouse' was a student or disabled. It also has a both-spouses-same-month limit that can affect the figures.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 19: 'No. Enter your spouse's earned income on line 19. If you or your spouse was a full-time student or disabled in 2025, see the instructions for lines 4 and 5'
findings.fix: Confirm that the filer's own student or disabled status is asked elsewhere for line 18. If it is not, ask 'Were you or your husband or wife a full-time student or unable to care for themselves in 2025?'

locators: p. 2, Married Persons Filing Separately, "If you don't meet all of the requirements to be treated as unmarried, you can’t generally take the credit. However, you can generally take the exclusion if you meet items 2 through 5"
p. 5, Line 19, "If you or your spouse was a full-time student or disabled in 2025, see the instructions for lines 4 and 5"
